A lifelong GH-receptor-antagonist transgenic (LIST2026; an earlier study of the same line did not detect extension) and a tamoxifen-inducible whole-body Ghr knockout started at 12 months (DUR2026). mTOR signalling was not measured in either, so the route through PI3K-Akt-mTOR is inferred, not shown here.

mechanism: Active mTORC1, acting through the transcription factor c-MYC, raises production of MAT2A, the enzyme that makes SAM, so a growing cell makes more of its main methyl donor.
mechanism_beginner: mTORC1 tells the cell to make more SAM.
boundary: Human cell lines and mouse xenograft tumours; acts through c-MYC on MAT2A. Together with SAM-SAMTOR this forms a loop whose behaviour in normal tissue is untested. Single study.

mechanism: PDCD4 binds the mTORC2 subunit Rictor through three basic residues, which stops mTORC2 from assembling properly and lowers its kinase activity.
mechanism_beginner: PDCD4 grabs Rictor and keeps mTORC2 from working.
boundary: Human NSCLC cell lines and mouse xenografts; not shown in normal tissue. Single study.

mechanism: When amino acids run out, the Rag GTPases also pull the TSC complex onto the lysosome, where it can switch Rheb off and help shut mTORC1 down.
mechanism_beginner: Without amino acids, the Rags bring the TSC brake to the lysosome.
boundary: Mammalian cell lines under acute amino-acid withdrawal; the contribution of this route in tissues is not established. Single study.

mechanism: When lysosomes are stressed, ULK1 (or its relative TBK1) phosphorylates FNIP1 at S296 on the lysosome. This switches the FLCN-FNIP complex off, so mTORC1 can no longer hold TFEB in the cytoplasm and TFEB moves into the nucleus.
mechanism_beginner: ULK1 tags FNIP1, which turns FLCN off and lets TFEB escape mTORC1's grip.
boundary: Human cell lines and ATP6V1B2-mutant follicular lymphoma samples; a nutrient-independent lysosomal-stress route, and TBK1 can substitute for ULK1. Single study.

mechanism: Akt phosphorylates FOXO transcription factors and excludes them from the nucleus. Rictor or mLST8 deletion abolishes signalling to Akt–FOXO while sparing S6K1.
mechanism_beginner: Akt tags FOXO proteins and keeps them out of the nucleus; this specific link belongs to mTORC2, not mTORC1.
boundary: Mouse knockouts and cell lines; FOXO isoform contributions differ by tissue.

mechanism: Insulin binds the insulin receptor, which phosphorylates IRS proteins; those recruit PI3K, which makes PIP3 and so starts the arm that reaches mTORC1 through Akt. The step is also where the pathway's best-known feedback lands: S6K1 depletes IRS1/2 and the cell goes deaf to insulin (SHA2004).
mechanism_beginner: Insulin lands on its own receptor on the cell surface. The message is passed inward by IRS proteins to PI3K, which builds a signalling lipid, and that is the beginning of the route to mTORC1. This is also the step that breaks when the pathway is overactive for too long.
boundary: Insulin and IGF-1 share this receptor arm; growth hormone does not, and is kept separate for that reason. The amplitude and the time pattern of the insulin signal are not interchangeable: KUB2012 shows the AKT pathway multiplexes insulin's temporal pattern, so a single arrow understates what the cell reads. Cell and genetic work, plus human physiology for the insulin-resistance end of it.

mechanism: TORC1 activity tracks ribosome biogenesis: in budding yeast TORC1 and PKA activity towards ribosome biogenesis oscillates with the cell cycle (GUE2022), and in mammalian cells the translational programme mTORC1 controls is dominated by the ribosome's own components (HSI2012). The dependency also runs the other way: when ribosome biogenesis fails, mTOR inactivation is what lets cells survive it (FAN2026).
mechanism_beginner: A growing cell needs more ribosomes, not just busier ones, and mTORC1 has a say in how many get built. That was followed through the cell cycle in yeast, and in mammalian cells the programme mTORC1 controls turns out to be dominated by the ribosome's own parts. The link runs in both directions: block ribosome building and the cell turns mTOR down to cope.
boundary: The two polymerase steps that carry most of this output are NOT measured by any study in this corpus. mTOR controls rRNA transcription through RNA polymerase I via TIF-IA (Mayer 2004, PMID 15004009, outside this corpus) and tRNA and 5S transcription through RNA polymerase III via Maf1 (Shor 2010, PMID 20233713, outside this corpus). Until those are curated here the edge rests on a yeast cell-cycle study, a mammalian ribosome-profiling study and a reverse-direction survival study, so read it as the existence of the output rather than as its mechanism.

mechanism: mTORC1 raises translation of the 5'TOP class of mRNAs, which encode ribosomal proteins and translation factors. Ribosome profiling showed the effect is selective rather than uniform: mTORC1 does not turn all translation up equally, it shifts which transcripts get translated.
mechanism_beginner: When mTORC1 is on, the cell does not simply make more of every protein. It preferentially makes the parts of its own protein-making machinery, from a particular class of messages marked at one end.
boundary: The selectivity is from ribosome profiling in cancer cell lines (HSI2012); the lifespan link is Drosophila only (WAN2026); PLEDGER2026 shows the same arm being repressed in chronically activated human CD8+ T cells. No human in vivo measurement of 5'TOP translation under an mTOR inhibitor in this corpus. Which of the 5'TOP transcripts matter for which phenotype is not resolved.

mechanism: Cholesterol binds the amino-terminal permease-like region of LYCHOS, and that is the step the sensing depends on: mutating the binding site impairs mTORC1 activation while leaving the protein in place (SHI2022). Occupancy switches LYCHOS into the state that holds GATOR1, so the sterol is read where it accumulates, on the lysosome, rather than at the cell surface.
mechanism_beginner: Cholesterol itself sticks to the sensor. That is what tells the sensor there is plenty about: break the spot where it sticks and the growth signal no longer goes through, even though the sensor is still there. The reading is taken at the lysosome, where cholesterol arrives, not at the outside of the cell.
boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus (SHI2022): human cell lines, photoaffinity and mutational biochemistry. The binding site was later resolved by cryo-EM outside this corpus (Bayly-Jones 2024, PMID 39358511; Zhao 2025, PMID 39824976; Li 2025, PMID 41058362). What is shown is that occupancy of the site is required for cholesterol-driven mTORC1 activation in cultured cells; no dose-response in tissue, no animal or human endpoint, and no measurement of how this route divides the signal with the SLC38A9-NPC1 complex (CAS2017).

mechanism: When lysosomal cholesterol is high, cholesterol binds the permease-like region of LYCHOS and LYCHOS binds GATOR1 through a conserved cytoplasm-facing loop. Sequestering GATOR1, which is the GTPase-activating protein for the Rag GTPases, keeps that brake off the Rags, so mTORC1 is recruited to the lysosome in a cholesterol- and Rag-dependent way. Mutating the cholesterol-binding site impairs mTORC1 activation (SHI2022).
mechanism_beginner: Cholesterol is a building block the cell needs to grow, so the lysosome keeps track of how much it has. When there is plenty, it sticks to a sensor protein called LYCHOS, which then holds on to GATOR1, the brake that would otherwise stop mTORC1 being pulled to the lysosome. Brake held out of the way, the growth switch gets to work.
boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus: human cell lines and biochemistry (SHI2022), with the binding interface supported by later cryo-EM structures outside this corpus (Bayly-Jones 2024, PMID 39358511; Zhao 2025, PMID 39824976). No animal or human endpoint, and no measurement of how much of lysosomal cholesterol sensing runs through this route as against the SLC38A9-NPC1 complex (CAS2017), which is a separate cholesterol input to the same machinery.
